extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students and practitioners of public relations researching press-release and crisis-communications history
extracted.subtask_description: Historical and practical principles for creating press releases and handling crisis communications, as illustrated by Ivy Lee's early-20th-century practices (e.g., Declaration of Principles, first press release after a train wreck, Rockefeller campaign). Useful for PR practitioners learning foundational norms such as transparency, truthfulness, and audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy, Authenticity, and Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Parker and Lee's agency boasted of 'Accuracy, Authenticity, and Interest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as the agency's founding boast—implies that communications (including press releases) should be factually accurate, genuinely represent the client, and be of interest to the public or press. No explicit scoring guidance; offered as foundational values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration of Principles — public responsibility beyond client obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Lee's 1906 'Declaration of Principles' articulated that public relations practitioners have a public responsibility that extends beyond obligations to the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed as the first articulation of ethical responsibility in PR—guides practitioners to consider the public interest and societal consequences when preparing press releases rather than serving only client spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely, proactive disclosure (preemptive transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: After the 1906 Atlantic City train wreck, Lee persuaded the company to disclose information to journalists before they could hear it elsewhere—often cited as the first press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example/precedent for issuing prompt, proactive statements to inform media directly and preempt misinformation or rumor during incidents. Implies speed and openness as key criteria in crisis statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the truth (honesty in communications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Famous guidance attributed to Lee: 'Tell the truth, because sooner or later the public will find out anyway.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advises honesty in messaging; coupled with the practical recommendation to change policies if the public disapproves. Note: the quotation's provenance is described as possibly apocryphal, but it functions as an ethical maxim for truthful press releases and long-term reputation management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way street approach — listen as well as communicate
rubrics_metrics.description: Lee espoused a 'two-way street' approach to public relations in which PR consists of helping clients listen as well as communicate messages to their publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages including mechanisms for feedback, gauging public sentiment, and adapting communications (and possibly policies) in response. Suggests press releases are one part of a dialogic process rather than one-way propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanize clients through personal engagement and visual documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Lee advised John D. Rockefeller Jr. to go personally to Colorado to meet miners and families, inspect conditions, attend events, and be photographed for press releases to present a more humanized version of the wealthy Rockefellers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates the tactic of using personal appearances, direct engagement, and photographs in releases to build empathy and favorable public perception. Example shows how narrative and imagery in releases can reshape public understanding of contentious events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis communications: rapid, ethical management to repair image
rubrics_metrics.description: Lee is credited as an originator of modern crisis communications, developing strategies (e.g., for the Rockefellers after the Ludlow Massacre) to repair public support by direct engagement and media outreach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies criteria for crisis statements: rapid response, transparency, humanizing actions, and strategic media use to rebuild trust. The historical examples illustrate strategic sequencing (personal action + press documentation) as effective crisis response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of internal publications and consistent stakeholder channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Lee pioneered the use of internal magazines, management newsletters, stockholder reports and news releases to maintain employee morale and communicate with different audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggests press releases should be part of a broader, audience-segmented communications program; maintain consistency across internal and external channels and tailor content to the intended stakeholder (employees, shareholders, media).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pro bono and public-interest work as reputational strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Lee did a great deal of pro bono work, which he considered important to his own public image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practice implying that engaging in pro bono or community-benefit communications/projects can strengthen credibility and reputation—an indirect criterion when planning public statements or releases aimed at reputation building.
